study.title: Jeremiah 25 The cup of wrath and judgment on Judah and the nations
study.overview: Jeremiah 25 presents a solemn turning point: after many years of warning, God declares that the time of tolerance has ended. The chapter recalls Judah's long resistance to the word of the LORD, announces the Babylonian invasion as an instrument of judgment and extends the scope of judgment to various nations. The central symbol is the cup of wrath: all nations designated by God will have to drink it, showing that divine judgment is neither place nor partial. At the same time, the text states that Babylon will also be held accountable, and that the Lord judges both his people and the neighboring peoples.

outline.title: Years of warning ignored
outline.explanation: Jeremiah recalls that for twenty-three years the LORD sent his word to Judah through him and other prophets. The problem was not a lack of warning, but refusal to listen, abandon the bad way and leave idolatry. Verse 7 summarizes guilt: the people transformed the work of their own hands into a cause for provocation against God.

outline.title: The judgment: Babylon shall come, and also fall
outline.explanation: Because Judah did not hear, the LORD lifteth Nebuchadnezzar and the forces of the north as an instrument of destruction. The earth will be in ruin, without joy or normal life, and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years. After that, the same God who used Babylon to judge will also judge Babylon for his wickedness, showing that the empire is not above judgment.

outline.title: The chalice of wrath for all nations
outline.explanation: Jeremiah receives a symbolic cup and must make it drink to a long list of peoples: Judah, Egypt, Philistines, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, the peoples of the wilderness, Elam, Media and other kingdoms. The image communicates disorientation, trembling and humiliation before the sword sent by God. The scope of judgment is universal, and the king of Babylon also appears among those who will eventually drink after the rest.

outline.title: Judgment begins with the city of God and reaches the whole earth
outline.explanation: Jeremiah must announce that no one will escape: if the city bearing the name of the LORD is already punished first, the other nations will not have innocence. The LORD is portrayed as one who roars from above and enters into judicial contention with the peoples, giving the wicked to the sword. The chapter ends with images of complete devastation, slaughtered leaders and ruined pastures; even the figure of the lion highlights the irresistible force of God's desolation.

study.context: The given notes place this prophecy in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, linked to the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, and point out that Jeremiah had already called the people to repentance for many years. Tyndale notes that Jeremiah's ministry began in 627 BC, which helps to understand the long divine patience mentioned in the chapter. The notes also indicate that the scene includes the ascension of Babylon as the dominant power and the scope of judgment beyond Judah, over many nations.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is patient, but not indifferent. The persistent refusal to hear the word divine brings concrete historical consequences, and judgment is not mere political chance, but the action of the LORD on history. In calling Nebuchadnezzar "my servant," the text shows that even pagan rulers can be used by God to execute discipline; this does not the inocenta, for Babylon also responds for its brutality and pride. The symbol of the cup teaches that the wrath of God is not whim, but a holy response to the rebellion and violence of the nations. The fact that Jerusalem is punished first reinforces the special responsibility of the people who bear the name of the Lord. At the same time, the chapter points to God's universal justice: no nation is out of its reach or above its assessment.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter highlights that the LORD was patient for a long time with the rebellion of Jerusalem, but finally the time of judgment came; the reference to the fourth year of Jehoiakim marks the beginning of the decisive action of Babylon against Judah.
When the people did not want to hear the word of God, they began to feel the judgments of his hand; the ruin comes because the warning was despised and the call to repentance was not answered.
The chalice of fury represents, in symbolic form, the universal desolation that would come upon the nations, and the image is explained as the sword sent by God among them.

questions: What in my life reveals that I hear the word of God in fact, and not just outwardly?
In which areas have I treated as it takes what the text shows to be serious: idolatry, disobedience and resistance to repentance?
How does the truth that God also judges nations and human powers corrects my trust in political or religious structures?
study.practice: This chapter calls to humility and immediate repentance. The concrete application is to examine whether there are habits, allegiance and practices that compete with obedience to the Lord, abandoning what is bad while there is still time to hear. It also invites us not to assume spiritual immunity: if Jerusalem has not escaped judgment because it was called by the name of the LORD, no one should play with divine discipline. Finally, he leads us to pray and act seriously before personal and collective sin, remembering that God's righteousness is real, comprehensive and upright.
study.uncertainty: Some historical details mentioned in the notes depend on chronological reconstructions and specific geographical identifications; therefore, they were used only when explicitly supported by the comments provided. The exact order of the chapter in relation to other texts of Jeremiah is presented in the notes as editorial observation, not as an internal certainty of the biblical text itself. The expression "Sesaque" appears in the biblical text, but the notes do not explain its meaning, so it was not interpreted beyond what is clearly indicated.
